preparedMetadata.title: How to store freeze-dried fruit after opening.
preparedMetadata.excerpt: Store no-added-sugar freeze-dried fruit in its original foil pouch. Avoid pantry decanting and ordinary zip-top bags, especially for apple and strawberry.
preparedMetadata.primaryKeyword: how to store freeze-dried fruit after opening

image.alt: A closed, unprinted silver foil-laminate pouch beside a small cream dish holding two freeze-dried strawberry slices and a pale apple piece.

changes: Reframed viral pantry-restock decanting as a reason to retain the original protective packaging, not to fill display jars.
Prioritized OhCrisp original aluminum-foil pouch; ordinary Ziplock-style bags, display jars and household boxes are not recommended as routine replacement storage.
Highlighted no-added-sugar apple/strawberry moisture exposure while retaining natural sugars and humidity/cut differences; no unsupported added-sugar protection claim or universal softening time.
Replaced the jar-led draft illustration with a closed opaque foil-laminate pouch and a very small immediate serving.
Synchronized excerpt, secondary keywords, visible image, alt, OG/Twitter/Article image metadata and generated pages.

sources.title: Implication of water activity and glass transition on the mechanical and optical properties of freeze-dried apple and banana slices
sources.supports: Original research: absorbed water and water activity affect mechanical properties of freeze-dried apple; no brand-specific open-air softening time is inferred.

sources.title: Water sorption isotherms and glass transition in strawberries: influence of pretreatment
sources.supports: Original research on moisture sorption and physical state in freeze-dried strawberry tissue; not a general added-sugar-versus-no-added-sugar comparison.

sources.title: Utah State University: Packaging Foods
sources.supports: Foil laminate reduces water-vapor transmission and original dried-fruit packaging is preferred when possible. The article does not misstate this source as proving all jars unsuitable.

sources.title: NCHFP: Packaging and Storing Dried Foods
sources.supports: Moisture reabsorption and spoilage precautions; no commercial after-opening shelf-life promise.

changes: Kept five flavor combinations and the three-role mix structure while removing blanket claims that fruit always keeps a mix loose or every piece holds its shape.

sources.title: FDA: Have Food Allergies? Read the Label
sources.supports: Review the full ingredient information each time; a Contains statement is not always present, and allergen advisory statements are voluntary.
sources.scopeLimit: No individual combination is described as allergen-free or suitable for a specific person; ingredient swaps alone do not establish suitability.

sources.title: The Hershey Company: Frequently Asked Questions (Products / chocolate storage)
sources.supports: Chocolate quality is sensitive to heat and humidity; warm conditions can cause melting.
sources.scopeLimit: Manufacturer guidance used as a named example; no universal exact melting/storage temperature or shelf life was copied.

sources.title: NCHFP: Packaging and Storing Dried Foods
sources.supports: Dry, tightly closed storage and moisture protection underpin the practical separate-component packing suggestion.
sources.scopeLimit: Wet/dry separation and mixing close to serving are editorial applications of moisture protection, not a tested snack-mix preservation process.
